newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INP says has 66.75 pct of Wilson & Horton.
newsitem.headline: INP says has 66.75 pct of Wilson & Horton.

text.p: Independent Newspapers Plc on Thursday said it had raised its stake in New Zealand publisher Wilson and Horton to 66.75 percent and confirmed it did not intend to raise the current offer.
"We've jumped ahead quite nicely now, we're up to just under 67 percent," INP managing director of international operations Brendan Hopkins said.

"That's a very important threshold for us because once we went over the 66 (percent mark), it's given us some very important tax advantages in terms of grouping," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Hopkins said the way INP had structured the bid, it received tax relief once it reached 66 percent.
INP is offering NZ$11 or 1.375 exchangeable INP shares for each Wilson and Horton share.
Hopkins said institutional shareholders were now starting to take up the offer, which closes on November 8.

"Traditionally what always happens is the institutions wait to the end...but as the price itself has effectively slipped back to our offer price in the marketplace, I think the general view now is that it's a very fair offer, and we're actually picking up shares not just from the written offer but also from the stand in the market," Hopkins said.
However, he said now that INP had gained enough shares to consolidate Wilson and Horton, it would be happy with less than 100 percent of the company.

"We obviously pitched the offer at what we thought was a very fair price and we'd be happy with whatever we end up with. Whether it's 70 percent, 80, 95 or 100...at all levels it works for us because of the way we structured the offer."
He said there were firm restrictions on what Independent could do to get more shares once the offer had closed.

"There are some very firm restrictions of five percent that you can buy in any one year. In fact, the way it is looking at the moment, our advisors are looking at this, it almost seems certain that we are already caught within the five percent rule, so we probably wouldn't be able to buy any more shares.
"We would actually have to launch a totally new offer, and with the cost of launching these offers, it's something that we probably wouldn't anticipate.
"We would actually probably have to wait about a year before we could buy more shares," he said.

"As far as we're concerned, if people want to stay in, fine, we'll accomodate them. It's not a problem, we're very used to having very significant shareholdings with minorities but at the same time we'll run the company obviously and we'll carry on and do what we want to do."
